newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIA BRACES FOR MORE PROTESTS, CLASHES.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIA BRACES FOR MORE PROTESTS, CLASHES.

text.p: Albanians vowed to keep up protests, one of them marred by a clash with club-wielding civilians, to demand that their government reimburse millions of dollars lost in dubious high-risk private investment schemes.
"Down with (President Sali) Berisha. We give you three days," several thousand demonstrators chanted in the southern town of Vlore on Thursday.
Anti-government protesters said they would stage a 10th day of protests on Friday in Vlore, the scene this week of some of the worst unrest in Albania since Stalinism fell in 1990.
"Unfortunately, Berisha is determined to go down a very dangerous path," said opposition Social Democrat party chief Medin Xhelili.
Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi have said they would return to luckless investors assets they were able to freeze in two collapsed schemes.
Frozen assets come to $300 million but much more is thought to have been lost. investors queued in Tirana to receive a 60 percent reimbursement from the two schemes.
In towns like Vlore, where the local "pyramid" scheme is estimated to owe $500 million, no assets were frozen and no one is expected to receive any money.
Berisha has offered to compensate losers with savings books, bonds or shares but such proposals have fallen on deaf ears. Albanians want their money back and they want it now.

"The government is going to find it very difficult to find that sort of money with the pressures it has on revenue. The sums involved are huge," said Heather Grabbe, a research fellow at London's Royal Institute for International Affairs.
"They seem to be in a no-win situation," she added.

Diplomats said the government was trapped between printing money to pay the hapless investors, which would wreck economic advances and trigger inflation, or to stick to its hard line and risk widespread social unrest.
Some estimates put loses as high as $2 billion, a sum about equal to Albania's annual gross domestic product.

The frustration of investors, many of whom sold houses or valuables to pile in to the schemes, prompted clashes between riot police and anti-government protesters in Vlore this week which left three dead and 150 injured.
Calm has returned after violent protests last month in many parts of the country but clashes and random violence were again reported in several places on Thursday.
European Union governments expressed concern over the new Balkan crisis and discussed ways to help Europe's poorest state head off a possible new wave of mass immigration.
The worst clash on Thursday was in the town of Fier, 120 km ( miles) south of Tirana, where civilians armed with wooden clubs and iron bars attacked seeral thousand protesters.
Witnesses in Fier said at least six people were injured. Three people went to hospital.
"We came out with flowers and they attacked us," members of the crowd shouted. Police at a nearby station stood by and did not intervene, the witnesses said.
Albania's main religious groups -- Moslems, Roman Catholics and Orthodox Christians -- agreed to hold a "day of prayer" for peace next Sunday.
